findings.paper_title: 3. Strategic Risk Scorecard Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: OneSAP ERP go-live completed successfully in March 2026, reducing execution risk
findings.detail: The major OneSAP implementation went live for Finance, HR and Payroll on 31 March as planned, with Ariba procurement functionality commencing 10 April. The programme had been rated Moderate 8 risk at start of quarter and is now reducing to target Low 4. Hypercare is underway and critical processes (payroll, payments, income) are stable.
findings.matters: This is a major operational transformation that underpins financial controls, HR systems and procurement. Successful go-live reduces a key technology and operational risk to financial management.
findings.figures: Risk downgrading from Moderate 8 to Low 4 by end of hypercare. First payroll for Gloucestershire Fire and Rescue Service completed successfully.
findings.quote: One SAP Programme went live for Finance, HR and Payroll on 31 March as planned with Ariba functionality commencing from 10 April. Hypercare has now commenced which is a period of enhanced support as the system beds in and users become familiarised. Regular payment runs are completing successfully.

findings.paper_title: 3. Strategic Risk Scorecard Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: Children's residential placement strategy faltering: fourth children's home project cancelled, new business case required
findings.detail: The council's planned four-home strategy for placement sufficiency is not proceeding. A new business case is needed, signalling delay to addressing capacity constraints identified in the Sufficiency Strategy. This is rated High 16 risk.
findings.matters: Insufficient placement capacity forces expensive spot purchasing from external providers and delays in moving children into appropriate placements, with financial and safeguarding consequences.
findings.figures: Risk rated High 16 (unchanged). Target Low 6.
findings.quote: The option for a fourth Children's Home located in the Forest of Dean is not proceeding and a new Business Case is required.

findings.paper_title: 3. Strategic Risk Scorecard Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: Home care capacity constrained: demand outstrips supply, forcing reliance on temporary bed-based alternatives
findings.detail: The council cannot support all adults who could live independently at home because demand for home care services exceeds available capacity. This forces the use of more expensive temporary respite and bed-based care as alternatives. Occupational therapy waiting lists have increased despite meeting KPI targets.
findings.matters: Unmet demand creates both service and financial risk: more expensive bed-based alternatives, complaints, and potential legal challenge if residents are placed in more restrictive care than necessary.
findings.figures: Risk rated High 16 (unchanged). OT meeting 95% KPI but waiting lists increasing.
findings.quote: Unable to support all those who can, to live independently at home, because demand for home care services outstrips available capacity. Resulting in the reliance on temporary respite/alternative bed based care in lieu of home care.

findings.paper_title: 3. Strategic Risk Scorecard Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: Explosive surge in EHCP assessment requests (200 in March 2026, highest since 2023 inspection) creating legal and cost pressures
findings.detail: SEND demand is rising sharply and now exceeds the council's ability to meet statutory timelines. The March 2026 surge (10% up on same month 2025) is attributed to the Schools White Paper announcement. The council cannot fill Educational Psychologist roles despite investment, creating delays. Parents are rejecting remote assessment options, slowing backlog reduction. This creates exposure to mediation costs, tribunal costs, and legal action.
findings.matters: This is a directly-funded statutory service where delay = legal liability and cost escalation. The council cannot control EHCP demand but must fund it, and cannot recruit the workforce to meet it.
findings.figures: 200 EHCNA requests in March 2026 (highest since 2023 inspection). Forecast to clear backlog by end September 2026. 50% of requests now from parents.
findings.quote: March 2026 saw 200 EHCNA requests, the highest ever since the SEND Inspection in 2023, and a 10% increase on the same month in 2025. This raises the rsik of increased pressure for Educational Psychologist advices, costs in mediation and tribunal risks with associated legal costs.

findings.paper_title: 3. Strategic Risk Scorecard Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: Adult social care provider market facing sustained fragility with high vacancy rates and rising operational costs
findings.detail: The market remains fragile with volatility in both residential and community care provision. Care homes face considerable pressures; vacancy rates remain high and operational costs are rising. A growing cohort of newly registered services remain unvetted by CQC.
findings.matters: Provider failure would force the council to step in immediately to maintain statutory care services, creating unplanned demand on reserves and operational capacity. Rising costs in a fragile market reduce the council's negotiating position.
findings.figures: Risk rated High 20 (unchanged). No quantified cost exposure given.
findings.quote: Care homes continue to face considerable pressures, with vacancy rates remaining high and operational costs rising, as confirmed in recent discussions at the Adults Risk Management Group and Performance Board. Alongside this, the wider adult social care market remains fragile, with ongoing volatility across both bed-based and community provision and a growing cohort of newly registered services that have not yet been inspected by the CQC.

findings.paper_title: 3. Strategic Risk Scorecard Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: High Needs Block deficit reduced by government support but leaves council with 10% unfunded burden
findings.detail: Government announced in January 2026 a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of the DSG deficit, reducing risk rating from High 20 to Moderate 12. However, the residual 10% remains a significant unfunded liability, and the timing and quantum of government funding is uncertain.
findings.matters: An unfunded 10% residual liability is material to financial sustainability and medium-term budgeting, and depends on government decisions outside the council's control.
findings.figures: High Needs Stability Grant covers up to 90% of deficit. Statutory Override ends 31 March 2028.
findings.quote: However, the funding of a residual 10% of the deficit still represents a significant unfunded burden for Gloucestershire, and the timing and quantum of High Needs Stability Grant remains uncertain.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Internal Audit Progress Report 2026-27
findings.headline: 31 audit recommendations remain open including 9 high-priority items, some dating to 2022-23
findings.detail: The audit committee is tracking 31 open recommendations across multiple audit years (2022-23, 2024-25, 2025-26, 2026-27): 9 are high priority, 21 are medium, and 2 are low. Several high-priority recommendations from 2022-23 remain unimplemented, nearly three years overdue. While the report notes a significant reduction in overdue recommendations since April 2024, the persistence of high-priority items indicates slower-than-expected remediation of identified control weaknesses. ARA is applying escalation processes to Directors and the Deputy Chief Executive for non-compliant action owners.
findings.matters: Open audit recommendations indicate the pace of control remediation. The number and age of high-priority unimplemented items suggests management may be stretched or prioritizing other work over addressing audit-identified risks.
findings.figures: 31 total open recommendations (9 high priority, 21 medium, 2 low); some exceeding implementation date by 12+ months; earliest reports from 2022-23
findings.quote: There are a small number of recommendations that have recently exceeded the target implementation date, and ARA continues to work with action owners across the Council to obtain the updates.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Internal Audit Progress Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Former council employee convicted of fraud by false representation and abuse of position
findings.detail: A long-standing fraud investigation concluded April 2026 with conviction. The defendant, a former council employee, pleaded guilty to two counts: fraud by false representation and fraud by abuse of position. The sentencing included 20 months imprisonment (suspended for 2 years), 120 hours unpaid work, mental health treatment requirement, and compensation of £3,600 ordered. The judge characterised the case harshly. The council identified and remediated the control failures in the affected area following discovery, indicating controls were insufficient to prevent or detect the fraud while occurring.
findings.matters: Demonstrates control failure that allowed employee fraud to occur undetected. While systems were strengthened post-incident, the case indicates potential vulnerabilities in the control environment that lenders assess when evaluating financial governance.
findings.figures: Compensation ordered £3,600; sentence: 20 months imprisonment (suspended 2 years), 120 hours unpaid work, mental health treatment requirement, rehabilitation activity requirement
findings.quote: A long-standing fraud investigation was finally concluded at the beginning of Apil 2026 with a successful court case. The defendant, a former employee of the Council, pleaded guilty to two counts of fraud: Fraud by false representation; and Fraud by abuse of position

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Internal Audit Progress Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards assessments not completed within statutory 21-day requirement, creating legal risk
findings.detail: Audit found DoLS assessments were not being completed within the statutory 21-day timescale. The audit flagged this as creating risk of individuals being unlawfully deprived of liberty, with explicit reference to potential financial and reputational damage. The council agreed to reassess cases, reduce waiting lists, and develop performance targets pending Department of Health and Social Care guidance. However, a Supreme Court ruling on 2 June 2026 fundamentally changed the scope by establishing that far fewer situations legally count as deprivation of liberty, meaning councils will undertake significantly fewer DoLS assessments going forward. The impact of this ruling on the council's workload and compliance position is still being assessed.
findings.matters: Statutory compliance failure creates legal liability. The council explicitly acknowledged risk of financial and reputational damage from unlawful deprivation. Though the June 2026 court ruling reduces future workload, the compliance gap currently exists.
findings.figures: 21-day statutory requirement (not being met); Supreme Court judgment date: 2 June 2026
findings.quote: DoLS were not being completed within the 21-day statutory timescale due to a number of contributing factors. This widely recognised national issue increases the risk of individuals potentially being deprived of their liberty unlawfully, resulting in financial and reputational damage to the Council

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Internal Audit Progress Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Build Back Better Grant Scheme audit gave Limited Assurance on £2 million allocation due to control weaknesses
findings.detail: The £2 million grant scheme (Cabinet approved, with councillors each awarding up to £40,000 in grants within their local areas) received a Limited Assurance rating from audit. Control failures included: grant documentation inconsistently completed and stored with missing councillor declarations of interest; sensitive financial information shared via unencrypted email; monitoring focused on outcomes rather than spend verification; variation in record quality; no reconciliation of payments to the council's financial system; and no risk register for the scheme. Audit raised 3 high-priority and 4 medium-priority recommendations. Although the scheme ended May 2025, audit noted these findings are applicable to other grant schemes within Adult Social Care, Public Health, and wider.
findings.matters: Multiple control failures on a £2 million discretionary spending programme demonstrate governance weaknesses, particularly in data security (unencrypted sensitive data) and financial tracking. The pattern identified could affect other active or future grant schemes.
findings.figures: £2 million allocation; councillors each awarded up to £40,000; 3 high priority recommendations; 4 medium priority recommendations
findings.quote: Sensitive, personal and financial information was shared via unencrypted email, increasing the risk of data breaches and non‑compliance with information security requirements

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 202526
findings.headline: Housing sector distress evident in council's £5m REIT fund, down from £5m principal to £3.2m
findings.detail: The council's social housing REIT fund fell 36% in value to £3.2m from a £5m principal investment. The fund manager attributes this to 'higher interest rates and associated debt costs' and notes that 'some Housing Associations within the sector are distressed as a result of poor management, high inflation, high energy costs and larger than expected voids.'
findings.matters: This signals stress in the housing association sector. More immediately, GCC has three £5m Rolling Credit Facilities with housing associations (Sovereign Network Housing x2, Moat Housing) currently undrawn but representing contingent exposure if these providers face financial stress.
findings.figures: REIT fund fallen from £5m principal to £3.2m market value (36% loss); three £5m RCF facilities with housing associations; total strategic funds showing £3.434m aggregate loss (£90m principal vs £86.566m market value)
findings.quote: Unfortunately, the value of this fund has fallen during the year to £3.2 million from an original principal value of £5 million, this is due to softening yields in the sector. Additionally, some Housing Associations (HAs) within the sector are distressed as a result of poor management, high inflation, high energy costs and larger than expected voids.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 202526
findings.headline: Capital programme expanding to £292m in 2027/28 while deferring long-term borrowing
findings.detail: Planned capital spend is accelerating (£142m in 2025/26, £224m in 2026/27, £292m in 2027/28) but the council is managing funding through short-term borrowing (seven temporary loans at 4.15%-4.7%) rather than securing long-term PWLB funding. The council explicitly states it will 'continue to be managed through short term borrowing, as long term PWLB remains expensive.'
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing creates refinancing risk if rates spike or markets tighten. The strategy defers expensive PWLB rates now but risks being forced to borrow at higher rates later if the conflict continues or gilt yields remain elevated.
findings.figures: Seven temporary loans taken May 2025 to February 2026 (four £10m, three £5m); rates 4.15%-4.7%; PWLB 10-year certainty rate rose from 5.38% to 5.72%
findings.quote: This position will continue to be managed through short term borrowing, as long term PWLB remains expensive in comparison to the LA to LA market.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 202526
findings.headline: Internal borrowing position explicitly identified as unsustainable
findings.detail: The council's Liability Benchmark analysis concludes that 'the internally borrowed position becomes unsustainable based on the current approved capital programme.' Current internal debt is £102.8m, with the net borrowing requirement forecast to nearly triple from £53.6m to £142.6m over two years, despite attempts to manage through short-term borrowing.
findings.matters: An explicitly unsustainable position means the council will eventually need to externalise borrowing at expensive long-term rates, or recut capital programmes. Either option signals constrained flexibility.
findings.figures: Internal debt £102.849m; net borrowing requirement: £53.6m (2025/26 actual), £88.1m (2026/27 forecast), £142.6m (2027/28 forecast); PWLB 10-year rates ranged 5.13%-5.88% during the year
findings.quote: This clearly shows that GCC has a funding need and the internally borrowed position becomes unsustainable based on the current approved capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 202526
findings.headline: Increasing SEND deficit is reducing investment balances and reserves
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies that investment balances have fallen by £8m during 2025/26 due to 'internal borrowing on the capital programme and the increasing SEND deficit.' This indicates a structural funding gap in Special Educational Needs and Disabilities that is consuming reserves rather than being funded sustainably from revenue.
findings.matters: SEND is a statutory service with growing costs. A council drawing down reserves to cover SEND deficits signals a structural imbalance that cannot be solved through reserve depletion alone and may force service cuts or further borrowing.
findings.figures: Investment balances fell from £201.5m to £193.4m (£8m reduction)
findings.quote: GCC has reducing balances due to internal borrowing on the capital programme and the increasing SEND deficit, both resulting in reducing balances and reserves.

findings.paper_title: GCC - VFM Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit of £124.7m identified as risk of significant weakness, exceeding available general reserves
findings.detail: The Council's cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit reached £124.7m at 31 March 2026, substantially exceeding available General Fund reserves. Government has announced support for up to 90% of historic deficits from April 2028 and ongoing cost support thereafter, but the Council remains exposed to approximately £12.5m residual local contribution plus any additional deficits accumulated before the statutory override expires in March 2028. Ongoing SEND demand pressures continue to drive deficit accumulation. KPMG has explicitly identified this as a 'risk of significant weakness' to medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A £124.7m liability substantially exceeding the council's general reserves represents a material financial sustainability risk; lenders must understand the residual unfunded burden and the council's dependency on government funding and statutory protections expiring in 2028.
findings.figures: £124.7m cumulative deficit at 31 March 2026; approximately £12.5m estimated residual local contribution; statutory override expires March 2028
findings.quote: The Council's cumulative DSG deficit increased to approximately £124.7m at 31 March 2026. Whilst the Government has announced support for up to 90% of historic deficits, and support for ongoing costs from 1st April 2028, the Council remains exposed to the residual liability and ongoing SEND demand pressures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Recommendation Monitoring – Overdue Recommendations
findings.headline: Rural Strategic Estate Plan review deferred due to Local Government Reorganization time constraints, with legacy 2016-2030 plan continuing
findings.detail: A high-priority (Feb 2026) audit recommendation to undertake a full review of the Rural Strategic Estate Plan was not approved in full. Instead, the council will continue delivering the 2016-2030 plan (now ten years old) alongside a more limited review of specific Task & Finish Group recommendations. Decision was made due to LGR time constraints. Final report expected Cabinet September 2026.
findings.matters: Strategic property planning underpins capital decisions and asset management. Operating a 2016-2030 plan in 2026 without full review, justified by LGR time constraints rather than asset assessment, suggests the council's strategic property position may not be fully current.
findings.figures: Plan original term: 2016-2030. Current date of decision: June 2026. High priority audit recommendation.
findings.quote: Accordingly, approval is being sought for continued delivery of the 2016-2030 SEP alongside a review of recommendations arising from the 2025 Task & Finish Group... the time restraints of LGR

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Recommendation Monitoring – Overdue Recommendations
findings.headline: SAP system implementation is causing cascading delays across multiple audit remediation workstreams
findings.detail: The Adult Social Care Debt Recovery SLA work has been delayed by SAP switchover, financial year-end, and global uplift (last update June 2026). The Bus Subsidy Grant audit trail work is tied to SAP go-live in April 2026 and will be reviewed post-implementation. Finance Procedure Rules updates were frozen pending SAP implementation in April 2026. Multiple updates cite SAP implementation as a reprioritization driver.
findings.matters: Major system implementations create operational risk and can result in control gaps or rework. A lender would want visibility on whether audit remediation and financial controls remain adequate during and after such a significant change.
findings.figures: SAP system go-live: April 2026. Multiple recommendations cite April 2026 as reset point or constraint.
findings.quote: Any changes to reoprting format in the SAP system will need to take place once the One Programme goes live in April 2026 because there is currently a freeze on any system changes to the existing SAP system.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Recommendation Monitoring – Overdue Recommendations
findings.headline: CIPFA Financial Management Code recommendations significantly overdue, with multiple financial governance actions not yet implemented
findings.detail: Four separate recommendations from the May 2025 CIPFA Financial Management Code audit remain overdue. Finance Procedure Rules updates are in draft and scheduled for October 2026 approval (originally targeted October 2025 then January 2026). Budget virements best practice guidance is still in development with completion expected September 2026. Financial management training for services and budget holders is partially complete (Finance staff trained post-SAP go-live) with service training scheduled June-July 2026 but originally targeted mid-2025/26. Finance performance reporting uniformity is in progress, expected end Q1 2026/27.
findings.matters: Multiple overdue audit findings on financial controls and governance infrastructure — particularly around virements thresholds, procedure rules clarity, and training — suggest control weaknesses. A lender would want assurance that the council's financial governance and internal controls are functioning effectively.
findings.figures: Target dates: Oct 2025, Sept 2025, July 2025, Oct 2025. Revised dates: Jan 2026, April 2026, June 2026, Jan 2026. Current status June 2026 shows all still pending.
findings.quote: Updates to the FPRs have been drafted, and will now be progressed through formal governance processes for full adoption. Update June 2026: Initial drafts of updates for Financial Procedure Rules have been prepared, and are being finalised. Scheduled for presentation to Constitution Committee for approval in October 2026.

findings.paper_title: SF25Jun26 2025-26 Outturn and Schools Balances 16 June 26
findings.headline: 36 maintained schools in deficit with £4.126m total revenue deficit, all on mandatory recovery plans
findings.detail: While Deficit Officers' intervention reduced schools forecasting deficits from 51 at the start of the year to 36 at year-end, 36 maintained schools still ended 2025/26 with a combined revenue deficit of £4.126m. All are required to submit recovery plans. The underlying driver is fluctuating or falling pupil numbers and increasing SEN within schools.
findings.matters: Distributed deficits across schools indicate financial weakness in the school system that may require council intervention and could create contingent liabilities.
findings.figures: 36 schools in deficit, £4.126m total revenue deficit, reduced from 51 schools forecasting deficits at start of year
findings.quote: only 34 of the 51 schools which projected a deficit position actually ended the year in a deficit. The total revenue deficit at year end for those 34 schools was £4m, however, 2 additional schools ended the year in a deficit position totalling £0.126m. This brought the total revenue deficit at the end of 2025/26 to £4.126m held by 36 schools

findings.paper_title: SF25Jun26 2025-26 Outturn and Schools Balances 16 June 26
findings.headline: High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of cumulative deficit is conditional on SEND reform plan approval by June 2026
findings.detail: The government announced a High Needs Stability Grant to cover 90% of the £124.718m cumulative DSG deficit (approximately £112m). However, receipt of the grant in Autumn 2026 is conditional on the council's approval of a SEND reform plan and supporting financial evidence by June 2026.
findings.matters: The council is dependent on securing this grant to manage the DSG deficit. If the reform plan fails to win approval, the council loses approximately £112m of funding support, creating a material gap.
findings.figures: High Needs Stability Grant covers 90% of £124.718m cumulative deficit (approximately £112m), conditional on June 2026 deadline
findings.quote: The condition of receipt of the grant in Autumn 2026 will be dependent on the approval of a SEND reform plan and financial evidence which needs to be completed by June 2026.

findings.paper_title: SF25Jun26 2025-26 Outturn and Schools Balances 16 June 26
findings.headline: Statutory Override allowing ring-fenced DSG deficit reserve expires March 2028, creating hard deadline for financial resolution
findings.detail: The council holds the £124.718m DSG deficit as a ring-fenced overdrawn reserve under a government-approved Statutory Override. This accounting mechanism expires in March 2028, less than 2 years away. Once it expires, the council will no longer be able to hold the deficit in this way.
findings.matters: Lenders must understand hard deadlines for financial resolution. The Override expiry creates a potential balance sheet crisis unless the DSG deficit is eliminated or the government extends the mechanism.
findings.figures: £124.718m DSG deficit, Override expiry March 2028
findings.quote: The Override expires in March 2028, but the impact on the Council's balances is significant with the deficit balance as at 31 March 2026 being £124.718 million.

findings.paper_title: SF25Jun26 2025-26 Outturn and Schools Balances 16 June 26
findings.headline: High Needs block £127.196m in deficit due to rising EHCP demand and unfavourable national funding formula
findings.detail: The High Needs block overspent by £46.693m in 2025/26, primarily driven by increasing demand for Education Health and Care Plan top-ups in mainstream and special schools. Gloucestershire, as a member of F40 (the lowest funded local authorities), faces a structural deficit due to an unfavourable national funding formula. The paper explicitly states deficits are predicted to continue into future years.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand that this is a structural, ongoing deficit driven by rising national demand for SEND support, not manageable overspending. Even with government intervention, annual deficits are expected to persist.
findings.figures: High Needs block £127.196m in deficit, 2025/26 in-year overspend £46.693m, cumulative DSG deficit £124.718m representing 17.2% of gross DSG budget
findings.quote: In year the High Needs outturn was in deficit by £46.693 million with the significant overspend due to the increasing demand for Education Health and Care Plans putting pressure on mainstream school and college top up budgets

findings.paper_title: High Needs Report - Schools Forum - June 2026
findings.headline: No long-term funding strategy articulated by DfE; council dependent on short-term grants and uncertain future allocations
findings.detail: The council explicitly notes that despite ambitious SEND reforms, 'we have not yet seen a long-term funding strategy associated to these reforms' from the Department for Education. The council is lobbying directly with the DfE and through the F40 group for a longer-term funding package. Current support is limited to short-term grants (Experts at Hand, High Needs Stability Grant) with no visibility beyond 2027/28.
findings.matters: The council is planning major service restructuring (specialist bases, inclusion, support models) without certainty about whether dedicated funding will follow. If the DfE fails to fund the promised reforms, Gloucestershire will absorb the full cost of the service expansion it has committed to.
findings.figures: High Needs Stability Grant applies to 2026/27 and 2027/28 only (90/10 split). Experts at Hand increases from £4.6m (2026/27) to £8m (2027/28) to £9m (2028/29). No allocations published beyond 2028/29.
findings.quote: Crucially, we have not yet seen a long-term funding strategy associated to these reforms, which shows how the DfE plan to invest money back into education settings to strengthen inclusion. We have details of short-term grants, but to deliver these reforms effectively, we need a longer-term funding package and financial strategy.

findings.paper_title: High Needs Report - Schools Forum - June 2026
findings.headline: £8m of deficit mitigation depends on completion of specialist capacity increases; these were planned before reforms and carry delivery risk
findings.detail: The council's strategy to manage the growing deficit relies on reducing demand for high-cost placements (independent school fees, bespoke SEND packages, and Education Other Than At School). The forecast assumes £8m of this mitigation will be achieved through increased specialist provision. However, this is described as 'existing mitigations that were planned prior to the SEND Reform announcements'—not new savings from the reforms themselves. Delivery of planned specialist bases and new special schools is the key to holding the line.
findings.matters: The council's deficit trajectory depends heavily on capex delivery (new special schools and specialist bases). If these projects slip or cost more than planned, the 2026/27 deficit forecast of £67.9m could widen materially.
findings.figures: £8m of high-cost placement mitigation. Specialist bases expansion planned from 80 to 560 places by end of 2029/30, alongside two new special schools adding 400 places.
findings.quote: Across both years the key mitigations relate to the increase in specialist capacity that reduces demand for higher cost placements, including Independent School Places, Bespoke SEND packages and Education Other Than at School (EOTAS). These are existing mitigations that were planned prior to the SEND Reform announcements and will mitigate around £8m of high-cost placements.

findings.paper_title: High Needs Report - Schools Forum - June 2026
findings.headline: Experts at Hand grant (£4.6m) carries hard deadline and strict allocation rules, creating time pressure and recruitment risk
findings.detail: Gloucestershire received £4.6m for Experts at Hand in 2026/27, with 80% mandated for direct delivery to education settings. The grant conditions require full spend within the financial year with no carry-over. As the report was written in June, three months into the financial year, recruitment into required specialist roles (educational psychologists, speech and language therapists, occupational therapists) within the compressed timeframe is flagged as 'challenging'. The council is exploring how to release existing capacity and use locum/interim support to accelerate deployment.
findings.matters: The council faces the risk of either failing to spend a committed grant (losing future funding) or incurring unplanned spend on high-cost interim staffing to meet the deadline. Both create budget volatility.
findings.figures: £4.6m Experts at Hand funding for 2026/27 (80% for direct delivery). Anticipated increase to £8m in 2027/28 and £9m in 2028/29. Report dated 19 June 2026, three months into financial year.
findings.quote: Recruitment into these roles in the time frames required is challenging, so we are exploring how existing capacity can be released and back filled with locum/interim support so that deployment can move quickly.

findings.paper_title: High Needs Report - Schools Forum - June 2026
findings.headline: Frozen High Needs funding meets 33% growth in mainstream primary school placements and 31% in secondary
findings.detail: Expenditure on mainstream primary school provision is budgeted to increase by £7.121m (33%) and secondary (pre-16) by £3.113m (31%) in 2026/27. This is happening with no increase in High Needs funding. The growth reflects continued rising demand for Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) on current trajectory.
findings.matters: The council is managing rapid service growth with static funding, indicating structural imbalance between need and resources. Mainstream school placements represent the single largest cost driver in the reforms and show no sign of moderating.
findings.figures: Mainstream Primary Schools: £7,120,989 increase (33%). Mainstream Secondary (Pre 16): £3,112,866 increase (31%). Total High Needs expenditure increase: £28.179m (19%). High Needs income increase: only £6.935m (7%).
findings.quote: This is underpinned by an assumption that the demand levels for EHCP will continue on their current trajectory. It should also be noted that there has been no increase in High Needs funding for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: High Needs Report - Schools Forum - June 2026
findings.headline: High Needs Block deficit growing: 2025/26 in-year overspend of £46.7m, forecast to reach £67.9m in 2026/27 on a cumulative deficit of £124.8m
findings.detail: The council spent £151.694m against budgeted income of £105.002m in 2025/26, creating an in-year overspend of £46.692m. The 2026/27 budget forecasts expenditure to reach £179.874m with only £111.936m of income, producing an in-year deficit of £67.937m. The cumulative deficit across all prior years stands at £124.8m.
findings.matters: The council is carrying a very large unfunded commitment in its largest statutory services. Although the DfE covers 90% of the deficit through the High Needs Stability Grant, the council must fund 10% itself (approximately £6.8–7m annually), which creates material pressure on the general fund.
findings.figures: 2025/26 outturn: £151.694m spend, £46.692m in-year overspend, £124.8m cumulative deficit. 2026/27 forecast: £179.874m spend, £67.9m in-year deficit, no increase in High Needs funding.
findings.quote: The final position shows a total spend of £151.694m, which resulted in an in-year overspend of £46.692m and a cumulative deficit position of £124.8m on the High Needs Block.

findings.paper_title: 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (COSC - Feb 2026)
findings.headline: Fire and Rescue Service forecasting £408k overspend including unbudgeted operational overtime and £175k one-off pension remedy issue
findings.detail: The overspend is driven by unbudgeted operational staff overtime, volatility of demand-led on-call service, and a one-off pension remedy financial liability estimate of £175k. A £100k growth item in 2026/27 MTFS is proposed but further work is required to confirm if the recurring overtime pressure is larger and how it will be managed.
findings.matters: The overtime pressure is flagged as potentially recurring but not fully quantified, creating uncertainty about future-year budget adequacy.
findings.figures: £408k forecast overspend; £175k one-off pension remedy; £100k proposed growth in 2026/27
findings.quote: Within the Fire and Rescue Service, there is a forecast overspend of £408k. This is due to unbudgeted operational staff overtime... a further one-off financial liability estimate of £175k related to a long-standing pension remedy issue... further work is required to confirm whether the recurring pressure is larger than this, and how it will be managed for future years.

findings.paper_title: 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (COSC - Feb 2026)
findings.headline: Savings programme 97.35% on track but £700k (2.65%) at amber or red risk including £158k Community Safety vacancy management and £100k education deferred pensions
findings.detail: Of £26.434m savings target, £5.889m fully achieved and £19.845m on target, but £192k is at amber risk and £508k at significant red risk. The red-rated schemes include £100k Education deferred pensions and £158k Community Safety vacancy management (of a £220k total target). These create budget pressures being managed through other underspends.
findings.matters: While the savings programme is mostly on track, the at-risk schemes reveal specific service area delivery challenges that are being masked by offsetting underspends elsewhere.
findings.figures: £700k at risk (2.65% of £26.434m target); £192k amber; £508k red
findings.quote: As at Quarter 3, £5.889 million (22.28%) has been fully achieved, and a further £19.845 million (75.07%) is on target to be achieved in 2025/26... Currently, £192k (0.73%) is at amber risk of not being achieved this financial year, and schemes totalling £508k (1.92%) are at significant risk

findings.paper_title: 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (COSC - Feb 2026)
findings.headline: Council has borrowed £40 million to cover liquidity shortfall with further £20 million needed before year-end and more expected in 2026/27
findings.detail: The liability benchmark analysis shows the council needs a minimum £82.4 million to maintain liquidity. Due to higher fixed borrowing costs, the council is keeping borrowing short-term. £40m has been borrowed to date with £20m more forecast needed before year-end and the balance expected early in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Structural liquidity pressure requiring sustained short-term borrowing indicates cash flow misalignment between receipts and commitments, particularly driven by DSG and reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: £40m borrowed to date; £20m more forecast to year-end; £82.4m minimum needed for liquidity
findings.quote: Analysis shows that we will need to borrow a minimum £82.4 million to maintain liquidity based on current forecasts. To date £40 million has been borrowed to cover this liquidity shortfall and another £20 million is forecast to be needed before the end of the financial year

findings.paper_title: 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (COSC - Feb 2026)
findings.headline: General Fund Reserve forecast at £36.322 million, marginal above minimum safe level of 5% at 5.2% of net budget
findings.detail: The General Fund Reserve is forecast at exactly the boundary of what the Council's Reserve Strategy considers minimum adequate. With £58.6m of other reserves being drawn down across the year and structural pressures in ASC, DSG, and highways, there is minimal buffer for unexpected costs.
findings.matters: Reserves at minimum safe levels limit the council's ability to manage unexpected pressures or absorb one-off costs, increasing borrowing dependency.
findings.figures: GF Reserve £36.322m; 5.2% of net budget 2026/27 (£694.940m); minimum policy threshold 5%
findings.quote: The forecast balance of the GF Reserve at 31 March 2026 would equate to circa 5.2% of the net budget, marginally above the minimum level (5%) set out in the Council's Reserve Strategy

findings.paper_title: 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (COSC - Feb 2026)
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £2.510 million driven by external placement costs and mental health demand, with investment fund slippage only partial mitigation
findings.detail: The overspend is driven by £3.461m in third-party placement costs (both demand and fees) and £1.297m mental health overspend relating to demand and complexity. This is only partially offset by £1.893m slippage in investment fund spending. A £3m growth bid for 2026/27 is proposed to address underlying pressure.
findings.matters: Despite the relatively small net overspend, the underlying cost pressures in placement services are substantial, and future solutions rely on growth bids being approved.
findings.figures: £2.510m net overspend; £3.461m placement costs; £1.297m mental health overspend
findings.quote: Adult Social Care (ASC) is reporting an overspend of £2.510 million at the end of Quarter 3... cost pressures within External Care Budgets (including the Transforming Care Programme): £3.461 million in respect third party / placement costs, both demand and average fees. Mental Health overspend of £1.297 million relating to demand and complexity.

findings.paper_title: 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (COSC - Feb 2026)
findings.headline: Irrecoverable insurance claims for road and bridge damage forecast at £561k due to increasing uninsured drivers
findings.detail: Street lighting and bridge damage caused by uninsured drivers is creating an ongoing budget pressure, expected to continue in future years. This is now considered manageable from departmental budgets but flagged as requiring monitoring through future MTFS processes.
findings.matters: This represents a form of revenue drain that the council cannot control or recover, reducing effective spending capacity.
findings.figures: £561k irrecoverable insurance claims forecast; trend expected to continue
findings.quote: irrecoverable insurance claims against damage to bridges and street lighting which will continue to be a budget pressure due to the increasing number of drivers without insurance who are damaging GCC assets

findings.paper_title: 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (COSC - Feb 2026)
findings.headline: Highways experiencing £943k gross overspend from cold weather damage and inflationary pressures on contracts
findings.detail: The overspend relates to an increased number of defects on roads requiring repair following cold weather earlier in the year, combined with above-budget contract inflationary pressures including changes to Employer National Insurance Contributions. Demand pressures can only be partially offset by £564k from commuted sums reserve, leaving £379k net overspend in year.
findings.matters: Uncontrollable external pressures (weather, inflation) are consuming reserves and creating recurrent budget pressure. The council has limited mitigation.
findings.figures: £943k gross overspend; £564k funded from commuted sums reserve; £379k net overspend
findings.quote: Highways movement relates to a gross overspend of £943k against environment and routine maintenance due to a combination of increased number of defects on the roads that required repairing as a consequence of the cold weather earlier in the year; as well as above budget contract inflationary pressures

findings.paper_title: 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (COSC - Feb 2026)
findings.headline: High Needs block pressure intensified by surge in demand for Education, Health and Care Plans and specialist placements
findings.detail: A review of activity trends showed increased overall demand for support and increased demand for more specialist support outside mainstream provision. This has led to significant increase in forecast projections in the High Needs block since the £30.3m budgeted deficit approved in February 2025. Cost pressures include mainstream school top-ups, special school and college top-ups, and independent special school placements.
findings.matters: Demand-driven deficits that cannot be controlled by efficiency savings indicate structural funding inadequacy and rising service pressure.
findings.figures: In-year DSG deficit increased from £30.3m budgeted to £45.550m forecast
findings.quote: A review of the activity trends for Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) this year has showed an increase in overall demand for support and also an increase in demand for more specialist support outside mainstream provision. This has led to the significant increase in forecast projections in the High Needs block for 2025/26

findings.paper_title: 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (COSC - Feb 2026)
findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit forecast to reach £124 million by March 2026, with statutory override expiring March 2028 and government funding solution still unclear
findings.detail: The DSG cumulative deficit was £78.537m at 1 April 2025. The in-year deficit forecast is £45.550m, bringing the total to £124.087m by year-end. Although Government announced in November 2025 that it intends to absorb SEND costs from 2028/29, it is unclear how it will address the historic deficits accumulated up to March 2028 when the override expires.
findings.matters: This is a ring-fenced statutory deficit that cannot be managed through normal reserves. The timeline creates a critical cliff-edge in three years with no confirmed solution.
findings.figures: DSG cumulative deficit £124.087m at 31 March 2026; override expires March 2028
findings.quote: The DSG cumulative deficit as at 1 April 2025 was £78.537 million... Government announced as part of its Budget proposals on 26 November 2025 that it intends to absorb SEND costs from Government budgets from 2028/29. However, it is unclear at this stage how Government intends to address the current in-year deficits and historic deficits accumulated up to 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: MTFS covering report - February 26 Full Council
findings.headline: Capital programme of £848.3m includes £39.4m of priority schemes funded from borrowing and revenue reserves
findings.detail: The four-year capital programme totals £848.3m, including £292.7m of new investment across services. Of the new schemes, £39.4m of priority schemes without grant funding are to be financed from borrowing and revenue reserves, while £51.2m of existing schemes are being removed.
findings.matters: Borrowing £39.4m for capital schemes will increase debt servicing requirements and could constrain future borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £848.3m total capital programme; £292.7m new investment; £39.4m funded from borrowing/reserves; £51.2m schemes removed
findings.quote: Priority schemes not supported by grants or contributions have been included within the new programme on the basis that they will be funded from borrowing and revenue reserves. These new schemes recommended for approval amount to £39.4 million and are detailed in Annex 8b.

findings.paper_title: MTFS covering report - February 26 Full Council
findings.headline: Medium-term plan with certainty only for year 1; years 2–3 indicative and year 4 a projection
findings.detail: Forward revenue budgets of £714.8m (2027/28), £734.1m (2028/29), and £769.3m (2029/30) are part of a 3-year settlement that provides certainty only to 2028/29. Years 2 and 3 are indicative, the government reserves the right to review them, and year 4 is a pure projection.
findings.matters: A 4-year plan with certainty only for year 1 creates significant planning risk and potential mid-period budget corrections.
findings.quote: The Provisional Local Government Settlement is a 3-year Settlement, which gives some certainty about resources to 2028/29. However, years 2 and 3 are indicative, and Government reserves the right to review these in the coming years. Year 4 (2029/30) is a projection.

findings.paper_title: MTFS covering report - February 26 Full Council
findings.headline: Council Tax increase of 4.99% using both general and Adult Social Care precept levers to balance budget
findings.detail: The proposed 2026/27 budget of £698.398m is based on a Council Tax increase of 4.99%, comprised of a 2.99% general increase plus a 2% Adult Social Care precept. This raises Band D from £1,679.65 to £1,763.46, an increase of £83.81 per annum.
findings.matters: Having used both available Council Tax levers to balance 2026/27, the council has limited options for revenue-raising if future deficits arise.
findings.figures: 4.99% total increase; 2.99% general increase; 2% ASC precept; Band D rises from £1,679.65 to £1,763.46
findings.quote: The proposed general fund revenue budget for 2026/27 totals £698.398 million and is based on an overall Council Tax increase of 4.99% (consisting of 2.99% general Council Tax increase plus a 2% Adult Social Care (ASC) Precept increase).

findings.paper_title: MTFS covering report - February 26 Full Council
findings.headline: High Needs Stability Grant contingent on SEND reform plan approval with no guarantee of support beyond 2027/28
findings.detail: Government will provide the High Needs Stability Grant covering up to 90% of the council's eligible ring-fenced cumulative DSG deficit, but receipt in Autumn 2026 requires Department of Education approval of a local SEND reform plan. Government has stated it will take an 'appropriate approach' for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits 'though it will not be unlimited'.
findings.matters: If the SEND reform plan is not approved or government support ends after 2027/28, the council could face an unmanageable deficit of over £241.6m.
findings.figures: Up to 90% of eligible ring-fenced cumulative deficit as at 31 March 2026; expected Autumn 2026 receipt
findings.quote: The HNSG is expected to be received in Autumn 2026, subject to GCC submitting and securing the Department of Education's approval of a local SEND reform plan. Government has also stated that it will take an appropriate approach for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits, 'though it will not be unlimited'.

findings.paper_title: MTFS covering report - February 26 Full Council
findings.headline: High Needs DSG deficit forecast to exceed £241.6m by March 2028 without external support
findings.detail: Gloucestershire's High Needs block is in deficit with £124.1m forecast as at 31 March 2026 and a £54.4m deficit budget for 2026/27. Without the proposed High Needs Stability Grant, the cumulative deficit is projected to grow beyond £241.6m by the end of the Statutory Override on 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: A £241.6m cumulative DSG deficit would represent a major unresolved funding gap that could threaten the council's financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £124.1m deficit as at 31 March 2026; £54.4m deficit budget in 2026/27; cumulative deficit projected to exceed £241.6m by 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The forecast deficit balance as at 31 March 2026 is £124.1 million. Based on current information it is anticipated that a deficit budget of £54.4 million will be set in 2026/27. In the absence of projections for potential HNSG receivable, the cumulative deficit is projected to grow to beyond £241.6 million by the expected end of Statutory Override on 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - S151 Officer Review of the Budget - S25 Statement
findings.headline: Government SEND funding solution is conditional on council approval and timing is uncertain
findings.detail: The Government has committed to a High Needs Stability Grant (HNSG) during 2026/27, covering up to 90% of eligible cumulative DSG deficit. However, receipt is 'subject to GCC submitting and securing the Department of Education's approval of a local SEND reform plan' and is 'expected in Autumn 2026.' The CFO notes that 'further detail is required around expectations of the local plan' and has not adjusted MTFS projections to reflect this uncertain funding.
findings.matters: A material funding assumption depends on both council approval by the Department and on timing that may not align with budget needs. Uncertainty means this cannot be relied upon for planning.
findings.figures: Up to 90% of eligible cumulative deficit as at 31 March 2026; expected receipt Autumn 2026
findings.quote: The HNSG is expected to be received in Autumn 2026, subject to GCC submitting and securing the Department of Education's approval of a local SEND reform plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - S151 Officer Review of the Budget - S25 Statement
findings.headline: £0.8m of unearmarked reserves drawn down to balance 2026/27 budget; CFO states this is 'acceptable but not sustainable'
findings.detail: The council is using £0.8m of unearmarked reserves to balance the 2026/27 budget. The CFO explicitly describes this as 'acceptable but not sustainable' and notes that reserves have 'very limited headroom.' With reduced contingencies, reserves now carry 'a greater burden in managing volatility and must be preserved for genuine risk events.'
findings.matters: The CFO is signalling that this level of reserve depletion cannot continue. Limited headroom reduces flexibility to absorb future shocks without borrowing.
findings.figures: £0.8m net use of unearmarked reserves; General Reserves remain above 5% minimum but with reduced headroom
findings.quote: Net planned use of £0.8m unearmarked reserves to balance the 2026/27 budget is acceptable but not sustainable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - S151 Officer Review of the Budget - S25 Statement
findings.headline: Risk profile has increased materially for 2026/27 due to late funding notification and reduced contingencies
findings.detail: The CFO explicitly states that 'GCC's risk profile has increased materially for 2026/27' due to late Government funding notification requiring rapid budget adjustments, reduced corporate contingencies for pay and inflation, continuing demand volatility, and structural SEND imbalance. The CFO frames this as 'now significant for GCC.' CIPFA's guidance specifically warns that late funding announcements and constrained contingencies heighten the probability of overspends.
findings.matters: Material increase in budget risk signals higher probability of budget failure and limits the council's ability to absorb emerging pressures mid-year.
findings.figures: Risk assessment in Annex 5; contingencies reduced following late funding settlement
findings.quote: CIPFA's guidance warns CFOs to recognise where late funding announcements or constrained contingencies materially heighten the probability of overspends. This risk is now significant for GCC.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - S151 Officer Review of the Budget - S25 Statement
findings.headline: The S151 Officer's assurance is explicitly conditional on Government implementing a fully funded SEND solution by March 2028
findings.detail: The CFO states that his Section 25 assurance is conditional on two things: (1) the DSG Statutory Override remaining in place until March 2028, and (2) Government implementing a fully funded national solution to both historic SEND deficits and revenue costs. The CFO explicitly warns that if these assumptions are not met, 'GCC's ability to remain financially sustainable in the medium term would be fundamentally undermined, and alternative approaches to maintaining solvency would need to be considered.'
findings.matters: The CFO is signalling that solvency assurance is contingent on external Government action. Failure to meet these assumptions would require fundamental changes to the council's financial management.
findings.figures: Contingency dependent on DSG Override to March 2028 and fully funded Government solution
findings.quote: If these assumptions are not met, GCC's ability to remain financially sustainable in the medium term would be fundamentally undermined, and alternative approaches to maintaining solvency would need to be considered.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - S151 Officer Review of the Budget - S25 Statement
findings.headline: Gloucestershire holds £124.1m cumulative SEND/DSG deficit—the council's single most material financial risk
findings.detail: The council has accumulated £124.1m of unfunded expenditure on statutory SEND duties by March 2026. This is framed as 'the Council's single most significant financial risk.' Sector-wide SEND deficits are modelled to reach approximately £14bn by March 2028 when the statutory override protecting councils from this deficit expires. Without a national Government solution before that date, most affected councils, including Gloucestershire, would face Section 114 (insolvency) notices.
findings.matters: This is an existential solvency risk. The council's ability to continue operating depends entirely on Government intervention—a dependency explicitly flagged by the CFO.
findings.figures: £124.1m cumulative deficit by March 2026; estimated £14bn sector-wide deficits by March 2028
findings.quote: By March 2026, Gloucestershire County Council (GCC) is forecast to hold approximately £124.1 million of cumulative DSG/SEND deficit arising from unfunded expenditure on statutory SEND duties. This represents the Council's single most significant financial risk.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: Reliance on reserve drawdown to balance budget: £0.8 million in 2026/27, £4.2 million in 2027/28
findings.detail: The council is unable to balance its budget from recurring revenue sources alone. It is using £0.8 million of unearmarked reserves in 2026/27 and £4.2 million in 2027/28 to close budget gaps. This is consuming reserves that should be held for contingencies.
findings.matters: Recurring use of reserves indicates the council's recurring budget is not balanced. Reserves are being depleted to smooth the impact of structural funding shortfalls. This is unsustainable and leaves the council vulnerable to any service demand spike or funding reduction.
findings.figures: 2026/27 reserve use: £0.8 million; 2027/28 reserve use: £4.2 million
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget proposals are balanced with a net transfer from reserves of £0.8 million. The 2027/28 budget proposals are also balanced following the use of £4.2 million use of non-earmarked reserves to fund one-off pressures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: Grant framework consolidation still being assessed; further impacts may arise through confirmation of new conditions
findings.detail: The government has consolidated 16 grants into 4 new consolidated grants and consolidated 17 funding streams into Revenue Support Grant. Gloucestershire has not yet worked through the full implications. The document notes that the full implications are still being reviewed and risks remain from future confirmation of specific terms and conditions.
findings.matters: The council is operating under significant uncertainty. Hidden unfunded responsibilities or changed conditions could emerge and create mid-year budget pressures or unfunded service obligations.
findings.figures: 16 grants consolidated into 4 new grants; 17 funding streams consolidated into RSG
findings.quote: The full implications of the changes to the grant framework and the new consolidated grants on the Budget is still being reviewed. Information on new responsibilities is being sought to ensure that appropriate plans can be put into place. Given the significant impact of changes to grants for 2026/27 announced as part of the Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement, there remains a risk that further impacts may arise in future years, and/or through confirmation of the specific terms and conditions of new grants.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: Council tax dependency increasing: 63% of base budget in 2026/27, forecast to reach 68% by 2028/29
findings.detail: Due to the fair funding redistribution, Gloucestershire's reliance on council tax is increasing substantially. In 2026/27, 63% of the base budget is funded from council tax. This is forecast to increase to 68% by 2028/29. The council is raising council tax by the maximum permissible 4.99% (2.99% general increase plus 2% adult social care precept).
findings.matters: As a council becomes increasingly dependent on local tax revenue rather than government grant, it becomes more exposed to local taxpayer resistance and less able to respond to demand increases or central policy changes. At 68% council tax dependency, the council is reliant on a taxation source it cannot easily expand beyond the referendum limit.
findings.figures: Council tax funding 2026/27: 63% of base budget; forecast 2028/29: 68%; 2026/27 increase 4.99% (2.99% + 2% ASC precept)
findings.quote: With the changes to the funding system this is even more apparent with 63% of GCC's base budget being funded from Council Tax in 2026/27, forecast to increase to 68% by 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: School funding settlement shortfall requires cuts to the National Funding Formula
findings.detail: The school block DSG settlement in 2026/27 is insufficient to fund all schools at the 100% National Funding Formula level. There is a shortfall of £0.4 million that requires all NFF factor rates to be reduced by 0.0978%, affecting school budgets across the county.
findings.matters: The shortfall indicates central government is underfunding the school system. The council is being forced to reduce school budgets, which may trigger schools financial notices to improve or create complaints to elected representatives.
findings.figures: School block funding shortfall: £0.4 million; required NFF reduction: 0.0978%
findings.quote: The funds allocated in the school's block settlement in 2026/27 are not enough to allow funding to schools at the 100% National Funding Formula (NFF) level. There is a shortfall in the funding needed of £0.4 million which will require a 0.0978% reduction to the NFF factor rates.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block in structural deficit: £124.1 million as at March 2026
findings.detail: The High Needs Block of the DSG is in significant deficit. The forecast deficit as of 31 March 2026 is £124.1 million. The council anticipates this will increase to a £54.4 million deficit budget in 2026/27 and £63.1 million in 2027/28. The council is using a Statutory Override that allows it to carry a ring-fenced deficit, but this is not a sustainable position.
findings.matters: This £124m deficit represents unfunded demand for special educational needs services that the council is holding as negative reserves. The deficit is growing and DfE reforms announced for early 2026 may worsen the position. This is a live liability on the council's balance sheet.
findings.figures: DSG High Needs deficit 31 March 2026: £124.1 million; forecast 2026/27: £54.4 million deficit; forecast 2027/28: £63.1 million deficit
findings.quote: The forecast deficit balance as of 31 March 2026 is £124.1 million. Based on current information (without any resetting of the High Needs allocations) it is anticipated that a deficit budget of £54.4 million will be set in 2026/27 and £63.1 million in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: Unresolved budget gaps of £9.4 million (2028/29) and £9.6 million (2029/30) with no identified solutions
findings.detail: After balancing the 2026/27 budget through use of £0.8 million of reserves and 2027/28 through £4.2 million of reserves, structural budget gaps emerge in years three and four of the MTFS. These gaps of £9.4m and £9.6m respectively have no identified funding source or efficiency programme to address them.
findings.matters: The council's financial plan is not sustainable beyond year two without either significant service reductions, additional tax rises, or new funding. Lenders will be concerned about the absence of a clear recovery plan.
findings.figures: Budget gap 2028/29: £9.4 million; Budget gap 2029/30: £9.6 million
findings.quote: There remain budget gaps in 2028/29 and 2029/30 of £9.4 million and £9.6 million respectively, which will need to be addressed through additional funding and further efficiencies.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: True resource reduction of £9.5 million in 2026/27 growing to £34.9 million by 2029/30 from grant consolidation losses
findings.detail: Although the budget shows a £345k increase in Core Spending Power for 2026/27, this masks that specific grants worth £9.5 million have been consolidated into CSP or revenue support grant at reduced values. When measured against the responsibilities these grants were intended to fund, the authority faces a reduction that will grow to £34.9 million by 2029/30. The council is still reviewing the full implications of these changes.
findings.matters: The headline funding position is misleading. The council's actual purchasing power is declining significantly, and the council has not yet quantified all the unfunded responsibilities being transferred to it.
findings.figures: £9.5 million reduction growing to £34.9 million by 2029/30
findings.quote: Whilst the movement in resources reflects a £345k increase to CSP in 2026/27, specific grants are no longer available to resource key responsibilities as identified below, meaning the true impact to resources is a reduction of £9.5 million growing to £34.9 million in 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: Loss of £1.1 million annual business rates pooling income due to system reset
findings.detail: For over a decade, Gloucestershire has received gains from business rates pooling with its district councils. The 2026/27 reset of the business rates retention scheme has eliminated these gains entirely because levies are now standardised at 10% for all districts. The council received an average of £1.1 million per year from pooling, which now ceases.
findings.matters: This represents a permanent loss of recurring revenue of £1.1m annually. It is not recoverable through efficiency or management action, only through increased taxation or service reduction.
findings.figures: £1.1 million per year average gain from pooling now eliminated; £3.9 million average pooling gain across all councils
findings.quote: As a result, and following discussions with the districts no pooling application has been submitted. This is an unfortunate change to the system, as gains from pooling have been on average £3.9 million, with GCC receiving an average gain of £1.1 million per year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: Funding growth far below national average: only 8.3% over three years against national average of 15.5%
findings.detail: Nationally, Core Spending Power has increased by 15.5% over the settlement period, but Gloucestershire's increase is only 8.3%. This is particularly acute because the Fair Funding Review has redistributed funding away from county councils towards areas with higher deprivation. The council's core spending power is now funded by only 33% from government grants, forecast to fall to 28% by 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's financial sustainability needs to know its funding is declining relative to peers and increasingly dependent on council tax. This creates structural weakness.
findings.figures: GCC CSP increase 8.3% vs national 15.5%; government grants 33% of CSP falling to 28% by 2028/29
findings.quote: Nationally CSP over the period of the multi-year settlement has increased by 15.5%, however GCC is well below this at just 8.3%.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (Informal Cabinet - Clean) - Copy
findings.headline: Highways maintenance overspend widening due to weather damage and insurance claims totalling £1.6m
findings.detail: Economy, Environment & Infrastructure moved to a £100k overspend at Q3 (adverse movement of £372k from Q2). Highways is the driver: £943k gross overspend on routine maintenance from increased road defects caused by cold weather, plus above-budget contract inflation (including ENICs). Irrecoverable insurance claims for uninsured-driver road damage total £561k and are described as 'increasing'. Street lighting energy £479k over. These are being partially offset by commuted sums and parking income recovery, but underlying pressure is structural (climate, uninsured drivers, energy costs).
findings.matters: Highway maintenance is inelastic: roads must be kept safe. The combination of weather-driven defects, rising uninsured-driver liability, and energy inflation creates a cost base both growing and difficult to control. If this recurs next winter, highways will be a persistent overspend.
findings.figures: Q3 adverse movement £372k. Highways routine maintenance gross overspend £943k. Irrecoverable insurance claims £561k. Street lighting energy £479k gross (partially offset by reserves).
findings.quote: The Highways movement relates to a gross overspend of £943k against environment and routine maintenance due to a combination of increased number of defects on the roads that required repairing as a consequence of the cold weather earlier in the year; as well as above budget contract inflationary pressures. Highways budgets are also forecasting an overspend of £561k for irrecoverable insurance claims against damage to bridges and street lighting which will continue to be a budget pressure due to the increasing number of drivers without insurance who are damaging GCC assets.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (Informal Cabinet - Clean) - Copy
findings.headline: Children in care numbers continuing to increase, creating volatile budget risk in underspent service area
findings.detail: Children & Families is currently showing a healthy £2.9m underspend, but the report flags rising volatility in activity. Children in care numbers increased over Q3, UASC placements added 37 high-cost cases, and disabled children's care showed new pressures (£544k adverse Q3 movement). These variances are offset by recruitment slippage and children's homes staff delays. The warning is explicit: volatile activity is an 'on-going risk' that requires 'robust management', and the underspends are included in 2026/27 savings plans, suggesting the underspend may not recur.
findings.matters: Rising numbers in children's social care (children in care, UASC, high needs) are driven by factors outside council control. If current underspends are one-off or slippage, the service will face sudden pressure when caseload growth materialises.
findings.figures: Children & Families underspend £2.991m at Q3. UASC 37 additional placements Q2-Q3 (underspend only £851k, showing cost per child is high). Disabled children's care £1.943m overspend. Children in care numbers 'increasing over the last quarter'.
findings.quote: The volatility in activity trends and costs within Children's services is an on-going risk to the financial position with children in care numbers increasing over the last quarter. The potential risk to the budget will continue to require robust management to the end of the year and beyond. The significant underspends reported for external placements/Children's Homes, UASC and legal fees are included as part of the proposed savings plan in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (Informal Cabinet - Clean) - Copy
findings.headline: General Fund reserve at minimum safe level (5.2%) with no buffer for unforeseen pressures
findings.detail: The General Fund reserve is forecast to be £36.3m at 31 March 2026, which is only 5.2% of the £694.9m net revenue budget. The council's own Reserve Strategy sets a minimum of 5%. There is therefore no safety margin for unforeseen pressures (like additional ASC demand, DSG volatility, or capital slippage). Any adverse movement would trigger either service cuts or additional borrowing mid-year.
findings.matters: A local authority operating at the minimum safe reserve level has no flexibility to absorb new pressures without drawing on borrowing. This constrains financial resilience and makes the authority dependent on tight budget control and savings delivery.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve £36.322m (31 March 2026). Net revenue budget £694.940m. Reserve as % of budget 5.2%. Minimum policy level 5.0%.
findings.quote: The General Fund (GF) Reserve is currently forecast to have a balance of £36.322 million as at 31 March 2026. The expected net operating budget for 2026/27 included in the draft MTFS reported to Cabinet in January 2026 is £694.940 million. The forecast balance of the GF Reserve at 31 March 2026 would equate to circa 5.2% of the net budget, marginally above the minimum level (5%) set out in the Council's Reserve Strategy.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (Informal Cabinet - Clean) - Copy
findings.headline: Council has borrowed £40m to date for liquidity and will need at least £82.4m total to maintain cash position through 2026/27
findings.detail: Q3 shows a material shift in borrowing profile. The council has already drawn £40m short-term debt to cover liquidity shortfalls driven by reserve drawdowns (notably DSG). Forecast shows another £20m needed by year-end, with potentially £22.4m more required early in 2026/27. This borrowing pressure reflects both capital programme timing and the DSG deficit requiring reserve use. The council is deliberately keeping borrowing short-term (higher cost) to avoid long-term fixed rates.
findings.matters: Unexpected liquidity borrowing is a material change to financial position. It indicates cash reserves are not sufficient to cover planned drawdowns, and the scale (£82.4m minimum need) is significant relative to the council's revenue budget.
findings.figures: Borrowed to date £40m. Forecast need by year-end £20m more. Total minimum liquidity need £82.4m. Actual long-term debt £338.3m.
findings.quote: Due to the higher cost of fixed long-term borrowing, any borrowing need is currently kept short. To date £40 million has been borrowed to cover this liquidity shortfall and another £20 million is forecast to be needed before the end of the financial year, based on current cashflow forecasts. Analysis shows that we will need to borrow a minimum £82.4 million to maintain liquidity based on current forecasts.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (Informal Cabinet - Clean) - Copy
findings.headline: Savings programme underperforming: £700k (2.6%) of savings targets at risk of not landing
findings.detail: The £26.4m savings target is forecast to deliver only £25.7m (97.35%). Of the gap, £192k is at amber risk and £508k at significant (red) risk. Specific shortfalls include: £158k Community Safety vacancies (red), £187k Home to School Transport (amber), £250k corporate estate reshaping (won't be achieved due to ICB changes), and £100k education deferred pensions (red). The shortfalls are being offset by underspends elsewhere, but this is masking a pattern of savings not delivering as planned.
findings.matters: Savings shortfalls are early warning of budget control issues. When £700k of identified efficiency cuts fail to land, it signals either planning weakness or that service pressures are outrunning mitigation capacity.
findings.figures: Total target £26.434m. Forecast delivery £25.734m. At amber £192k (0.73%). At red £508k (1.92%). Community Safety vacancy target miss £158k. Corporate estate reshaping £250k (full shortfall).
findings.quote: Currently, £192k (0.73%) is at amber risk of not being achieved this financial year, and schemes totalling £508k (1.92%) are at significant risk of not being achieved. The schemes at most risk of not being delivered this year are: £158k of the Community Safety Vacancy Management target (target £220k) showing as high risk (Red rated). £250k of benefit realisation from reshaping of corporate estate. This will not be achieved due to changes with the ICB.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (Informal Cabinet - Clean) - Copy
findings.headline: Adult Social Care £2.5m overspend driven by placement costs and mental health demand, with £3m growth bid needed for 2026/27
findings.detail: ASC is overspending by £2.5m at Q3. The core issue is external care placement costs (£3.5m) and mental health services (£1.3m) both driven by demand and fee inflation. The council has submitted a £3m growth bid for 2026/27 in MTFS proposals, signalling this is structural, not one-off. The £100k improvement from Q2 came from ICB funding help, not resolved underlying pressure.
findings.matters: ASC is typically the largest and least-controllable spend line in local government. An overspend that requires a growth bid signals the council cannot absorb demand-led pressures from base budget, raising questions about sustainability of future positions.
findings.figures: £2.510m overspend (0.4% of service budget). Third-party placements £3.461m adverse. Mental Health £1.297m adverse. Growth bid £3.0m for 2026/27.
findings.quote: Adult Social Care is reporting an overspend of £2.510 million. The current overspend relates to cost pressures within External Care Budgets (including the Transforming Care Programme): £3.461 million in respect third party / placement costs, both demand and average fees. Mental Health overspend of £1.297 million relating to demand and complexity. The MTFS proposals include a growth bid of £3 million for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (Informal Cabinet - Clean) - Copy
findings.headline: DSG deficit forecast to reach £124 million by March 2026 with government solution still unclear
findings.detail: The cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is forecast to grow from £78.5m to £124.1m after an in-year loss of £45.5m (up £533k from Q2). This reflects surging demand for Education, Health and Care Plans and specialist provision outside mainstream schools. The government's Statutory Override protecting ring-fenced deficits expires March 2028, but ministers have not explained how the accumulated £124m will be addressed after announcing in November 2025 that SEND costs would transfer to government budgets from 2028/29.
findings.matters: This is the largest financial exposure on the council's balance sheet. Lenders and the finance director must know whether government will absorb legacy deficits or leave them with the council after 2028.
findings.figures: Cumulative deficit £78.537m (1 April 2025), in-year deficit £45.550m, forecast balance £124.087m (31 March 2026). Override expires March 2028.
findings.quote: The cumulative DSG deficit is therefore forecast to reach £124.087 million as at 31 March 2026. The Override expires in March 2028, but the impact on the Council's balances is significant. Government announced as part of its Budget proposals on 26 November 2025 that it intends to absorb SEND costs from Government budgets from 2028/29. However, it is unclear at this stage how Government intends to address the current in-year deficits and historic deficits accumulated up to 31 March 2028.

findings.matters: Significant committed annual cost increases in social care indicate structural service cost inflation that repeats every year and constrains budget flexibility.
